title: Real estate stocks: how to analyze property companies
description: Real estate stocks are valued on NAV, dividend yield and rate sensitivity — not the P/E. Here is the method, step by step, with examples and sources.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Real estate stocks are shares in companies that own and manage properties — residential buildings, offices, retail space and warehouses. Revenue comes mainly from rents, and earnings are shaped by how the portfolio is valued. That makes real estate stocks different from industrial companies to analyze: the P/E says little, and three measures take center stage — the net asset value (NAV), the dividend yield and the interest rate sensitivity of the debt.

This guide walks through what makes property companies special, step by step, with worked examples and sources. As always here: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What makes real estate stocks different

A property company's operations are simple to describe: buy, own, develop and rent out properties. The complexity lives in the accounting. Listed Swedish property companies report investment properties at fair value under IAS 40: each property is revalued continuously and the value changes — up or down — flow straight through the income statement. The same standard prohibits depreciation.

The consequence: reported earnings are to a large extent an accounting product. A rent increase or a falling yield requirement can lift the profit by billions without a krona being paid out — and vice versa. The sector therefore relies on cash-flow measures, above all FFO (funds from operations), which strips unrealized value changes out of earnings. Over time the share price follows the underlying cash flow and net asset value, not the reported profit. The sector's whole system of equations is built up in [the Real Estate Sector](/kurser/km-042-fastighetsektorn).

Put numbers on it: an example company reports an annual profit of SEK 1,200 million, of which SEK 800 million is unrealized appreciation. Cash flow from management is unchanged at SEK 400 million — and that item pays interest, dividends and maintenance. The profit tells what the portfolio has been valued at; the cash flow what the operations generate. The analysis needs both — kept apart.

## Dividend yield — the sector's own return measure

The dividend yield is the dividend per share divided by the share price. An example company paying SEK 4.80 at a price of SEK 96 yields 4.80 ÷ 96 = 5.0 percent. So you calculate it — and here the measure carries a double meaning: property companies price their own buildings as a yield (net rent ÷ property value), which ties the property's and the share's return measures together through the valuation.

The interest rate is the measure's constant benchmark: when rates rise, the market demands a higher yield on the real estate stock — and because the dividend sits in the numerator, the price can adjust downward mechanically. The reverse holds too: a sharply risen stock automatically gets a lower yield — the number says nothing about quality, only about today's pricing. A high yield is therefore not automatically a bargain; the control question is whether the dividend is carried by the cash flow — how large a share of FFO is paid out. That mechanism goes deeper in [equity and dividends](/kurser/km-005-eget-kapital-utdelningar) and [dividend strategy](/kurser/pf-05-utdelningsstrategi).

## NAV — the net asset value per share

NAV (net asset value) is a property company's substance: the market value of the property portfolio minus interest-bearing debt, divided by the number of shares. A worked example: properties valued at SEK 12,000 million and interest-bearing debt of SEK 7,000 million give a substance of SEK 5,000 million. With 100 million shares outstanding, NAV is SEK 50 per share. If the stock trades at SEK 42 it stands at 42 ÷ 50 = 0.84 in P/NAV — a 16 percent discount to substance.

The discount is not an argument in itself; it is the market's aggregated judgment of management, growth, debt and valuation credibility. The same substance logic applies to the investment companies Investor and Industrivärden — both are in AK1A's hundred-company universe and are valued against net assets, not operations. The whole argument on book-value multiples is found in [P/B — when book value is compared correctly](/blogg/pb-tal-nar-jamfor-man-bokvarde-ratt) and the course [relative valuation](/kurser/km-011-relativ-vardering). The industry association EPRA has standardized the net asset measures (including EPRA NTA) so that valuation assumptions become comparable between companies.

## Interest rates and leverage — the sector's Achilles' heel

Property companies are leveraged by construction: buildings are bought with a large share of the value in loans (in the example company the loan-to-value ratio is 7,000 ÷ 12,000 ≈ 58 percent; the level varies with company type and position in the property cycle). Three measures carry the interest rate analysis:

- **Loan-to-value ratio** — interest-bearing debt as a percentage of the property value. Higher leverage amplifies both the upswing and the downturn.
- **Interest coverage ratio** — operating profit before value changes divided by the interest cost. If the profit is SEK 900 million and the interest cost SEK 450 million, coverage is 2.0 times: the rate can double — or the profit halve — before coverage reaches 1.0, where profit no longer covers the interest.
- **Duration of the rate fixation** — determines how quickly a rate change feeds through to earnings. Long fixation periods brake the effect; short ones act fast.

The years 2022–2023 showed the whole mechanism in practice. The Riksbank raised its policy rate from zero to four percent between the end of 2021 and the autumn of 2023 — the highest level since the financial crisis — and real estate stocks fell far more than the broader market; the sector index lost almost half during 2022. Several companies were simultaneously forced into new share issues, diluting existing owners — that mechanism is walked through in [emission risk](/kurser/rk-02-emissionrisk). The interest rate side is systematized in [interest rate risk](/kurser/rk-08-ranterisk) and [debt-to-equity](/kurser/v10-skuldsattningsgrad), deeper in [which debt level is dangerous](/blogg/skuldsattningsgrad-vilken-niva-ar-farlig).

## How to read a property company's report

Start by placing the company in its segment: residential properties are driven by household finances and migration, offices by the labor market and workplace norms, retail and logistics by consumption and e-commerce's structural shift. The segments differ in vacancy drivers and contract structure — office leases renegotiate a few years at a time, residential rents move slowly through rent-setting models — which sets how fast the rental value responds to the economy.

The property report has its own key figures, separate from industry's. The most important:

- **Rental value** — the annual rental income the portfolio yields at current contracts; the sector's order book counterpart.
- **Vacancy rate** — the share of unlet space; every percentage point of vacancy is lost rent at almost pure margin.
- **Like-for-like growth** — rental development in the unchanged portfolio — growth not bought through acquisitions.
- **Net new letting level** — the rent level of new contracts minus moving, construction and vacancy costs; the sector's signature measure of demand.

Then read two places extra closely: the development projects — construction is different risk capital than management — and the notes on valuation assumptions: which yield requirement did the external appraiser use? That assumption drives the entire NAV. Always compare cash flow from management with reported profit: [cash flow analysis](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen) gives the method, [the quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten) the reading order and [the balance sheet in 15 minutes](/blogg/sa-laser-du-en-balansrakning-pa-15-minuter) the debt side.

## The summary

- Real estate stocks are analyzed against substance and cash flow: NAV and FFO replace the P/E as starting point.
- Dividend yield = dividend ÷ price; it constantly compares with the interest rate, and the dividend's sustainability is checked against FFO.
- Interest rate sensitivity lives in the loan-to-value ratio, the interest coverage ratio and the fixation period — the rate year 2022 is the sector's textbook case.
- The report's own key figures: rental value, vacancy rate, like-for-like growth and net new letting level — plus the valuation assumptions in the notes.

Two tracks continue: [the Real Estate Sector](/kurser/km-042-fastighetsektorn) goes deeper into the sector's measures, and a complete company analysis of a Swedish property company is found in [the NP3 Fastigheter analysis](/blogg/analys-np3-fastigheter-2026). How the sector is weighted into a portfolio is covered by [diversification](/kurser/pf-03-diversifiering).
